input: Teach myself touch typing using a free online tool

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Knowing whether they are a complete beginner or already have some typing habits changes whether the plan starts with home-row basics or jumps to speed/accuracy drills.
A target speed (e.g. 60 WPM) or accuracy level defines when the task is 'done' and shapes how long and intense the practice schedule needs to be.
The amount of time available per day directly determines how the practice sessions are structured and how realistic a timeline is.
The keyboard layout they use (QWERTY, Dvorak, AZERTY, etc.) determines which tools are even compatible and which lessons apply.
Knowing their age group or whether this is for professional, academic, or personal use helps tailor the tone and pacing of the recommended tool and plan.
Some people learn better with gamified, structured courses, or plain drills — matching the tool style to their preference increases follow-through.
Knowing the device they will practice on (laptop, desktop, tablet) rules out tools that do not work well on certain hardware and affects posture/ergonomics advice.

gold.taskTitle: Teach myself touch typing with free online tool
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to independently learn touch typing from scratch (or improve existing skills) using a free online resource.

questions.title: How would you describe your current typing ability?
questions.description: Are you a complete beginner who hunts and pecks, or do you already use some fingers consistently and want to refine technique?

questions.title: What typing speed or skill level is your goal?
questions.description: Do you have a specific target in mind, such as a words-per-minute goal, or is the goal simply to type without looking at the keyboard?

questions.title: How many minutes per day can you dedicate to practice?
questions.description: Your available daily practice time determines how sessions should be structured and how quickly you can realistically reach your goal.

questions.title: Which keyboard layout do you use — QWERTY, Dvorak, or another?
questions.description: The layout you type on must match the lessons offered by the tool, so this rules certain resources in or out.

questions.title: Is this for a specific purpose like work, school, or general use?
questions.description: Knowing the end use case helps prioritise certain skills, such as numeric keypad entry for data work or speed for academic writing.

questions.title: Do you prefer gamified lessons, structured courses, or plain drills?
questions.description: Different tools suit different learning styles — games like TypeRacer, structured courses like TypingClub, or minimalist drill tools each have distinct approaches.

questions.title: What device will you primarily practice on?
questions.description: Whether you are on a laptop, a desktop with an external keyboard, or a tablet affects which tools work smoothly and what ergonomic setup to recommend.
